lead: This unit turns a signal into its frequency recipe. You will write periodic signals as Fourier series and aperiodic signals as Fourier transforms, use transform properties, read energy and power spectra, and describe LTI systems by their frequency response. After it, you can test a channel for distortion, state ideal-filter specifications, compute correlations, and take a Hilbert transform.
about: The unit starts with Fourier series (3.1): a periodic signal becomes a sum of harmonics, in trigonometric or complex exponential form. Letting the period grow gives the Fourier transform (3.2) for aperiodic signals. Chapter 3.3 collects the transform properties, especially convolution and modulation. Parseval's theorem in 3.4 connects time-domain energy or power to spectral densities. Chapter 3.5 applies the transform to LTI systems through H(ω), and 3.6 uses H(ω) to define distortionless transmission, ideal filters, and realizability. Chapter 3.7 adds correlation and shows its Fourier pair with spectral density. Chapter 3.8 closes with the Hilbert transform, a −90° phase-shift filter.

chapters.idea: A periodic signal is a sum of harmonically related sinusoids, and the coefficients are found by orthogonality.
chapters.depth: Define period T₀, fundamental frequency f₀=1/T₀, and fundamental angular frequency ω₀=2π/T₀. Show orthogonality of cosines and sines over one period. Write x(t)=a₀/2+Σ[aₙcos(nω₀t)+bₙsin(nω₀t)] and x(t)=Σcₙe^{jnω₀t}; give the a₀, aₙ, bₙ and cₙ integrals, with cₙ=(aₙ−jbₙ)/2 for real x(t). State Dirichlet conditions and Gibbs phenomenon in one line. Cover properties: linearity, time shift, frequency shift, time reversal, time scaling, differentiation, integration, and symmetry for real even and odd signals. Some syllabi call the complex form the exponential Fourier series and the other the trigonometric form. Stop before Parseval; it comes in 3.4.

figure.title: Fourier series routes
figure.aria: A periodic signal gives Fourier coefficients through orthogonality; the coefficients build the exponential series and, for real signals, the trigonometric series.

chapters.example: For the periodic pulse x(t)=1 for −1<t<1 s and x(t)=0 for 1<|t|<2 s, with period T₀=4 s, find c₀ and cₙ, then write the exponential and trigonometric Fourier series. Answer: c₀=1/2, cₙ=sin(nπ/2)/(nπ) for n≠0; x(t)=1/2+Σ over n≠0 [sin(nπ/2)/(nπ)]e^{jn(π/2)t}; trigonometric form x(t)=1/2+Σ_{n=1}∞ (2 sin(nπ/2)/(nπ))cos(n(π/2)t), since bₙ=0.
chapters.trap: Dropping the 1/T₀ in cₙ or using ω₀=1/T₀ instead of 2π/T₀.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: periodic signals, even and odd symmetry, orthogonal signals.
chapters.leave: Parseval and power spectrum to 3.4; discrete Fourier series to Unit 6; Laplace to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An aperiodic signal has a continuous spectrum, obtained by letting the Fourier-series period go to infinity.
chapters.depth: Obtain X(ω)=∫x(t)e^{-jωt}dt from the series as T₀→∞. Give inverse x(t)=(1/2π)∫X(ω)e^{jωt}dω. State existence and continuity conditions briefly. Derive standard transforms: rectangular pulse ↔ sinc, impulse, constant, e^{-at}u(t), two-sided exponential, and periodic signals as impulse trains. Explain band-limiting versus time-limiting: a time-limited signal has an infinite spectrum and vice versa. Some syllabi write X(jω) instead of X(ω). Leave discrete-time transforms to Unit 6 and Laplace to Unit 4.

figure.aria: The magnitude of the Fourier transform of e^{-2t}u(t) starts at 0.5 and falls as frequency rises.

chapters.example: For x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t), find X(ω). Hence find |X(ω)| at ω=0 and ω=2 rad/s. Answer: X(ω)=1/(2+jω); |X(0)|=0.5, |X(2)|=1/√8≈0.354.
chapters.trap: Forgetting 1/2π in the inverse transform, or mixing f and ω.
chapters.leave: Properties to 3.3; discrete-time FT to Unit 6; Laplace and ROC to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Fourier transform properties turn difficult operations such as convolution and modulation into simple algebra on spectra.
chapters.depth: Cover linearity, time shift, frequency shift, scaling, differentiation, integration, duality, conjugation, and symmetry. Prove and use the convolution theorem x(t)*h(t) ↔ X(ω)H(ω) and the modulation theorem x(t)cos(ω₀t) ↔ ½[X(ω−ω₀)+X(ω+ω₀)]. Include the multiplication theorem in time. Use transform pairs and properties to compute transforms without integration. Some syllabi call modulation the frequency-shifting property. Leave energy consequences to 3.4.

figure.title: Two transform theorems
figure.aria: Multiplying a signal by a cosine shifts and halves its spectrum, while convolution in time becomes multiplication of spectra.

chapters.example: Find the Fourier transform of x(t)=e^{-2t}cos(10t)u(t) using the modulation theorem. Answer: X(ω)=½[1/(2+j(ω−10))+1/(2+j(ω+10))].
chapters.trap: Using the wrong sign in frequency shift: multiplying by e^{jω₀t} moves X(ω) to X(ω−ω₀).

chapters.idea: Parseval's theorem says the energy or power computed in time equals the area under the spectral density.
chapters.depth: Define energy E=∫|x(t)|²dt for energy signals and average power P=lim(1/T)∫|x(t)|²dt for power signals. State Parseval: E=(1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω and, for periodic signals, P=Σ|cₙ|². Define energy spectral density ESD=|X(ω)|² and power spectral density PSD. Show total energy or power as area under the density. Explain bandwidth from cumulative energy in one line. Leave autocorrelation relation to 3.7.

figure.aria: For x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t), the energy spectral density 1/(9+ω²) peaks at ω=0 and its area equals the energy 1/6 J.

chapters.example: For x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t), compute E=∫|x(t)|²dt and verify Parseval using X(ω)=1/(3+jω). Answer: E=∫_{0}^{∞}e^{-6t}dt=1/6 J; (1/2π)∫_{−∞}^{∞}1/(9+ω²)dω=(1/2π)(π/3)=1/6 J.
chapters.trap: Missing 1/2π in Parseval or calling |X(ω)|² power when x is an energy signal.
chapters.prereq: 3.1–3.3; energy and power signals from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Autocorrelation and PSD relation to 3.7; random signals out.

chapters.idea: An LTI system scales and phase-shifts each frequency by H(ω), so its sinusoidal steady-state output follows directly from |H| and ∠H.
chapters.depth: Define H(ω)=Y(ω)/X(ω)=FT{h(t)}. Give magnitude |H(ω)| and phase ∠H(ω). For sinusoidal input A cos(ω₀t+φ), output is A|H(ω₀)|cos(ω₀t+φ+∠H(ω₀)). Compute H(ω) from impulse response or differential equation. Draw magnitude and phase sketches; no log scales needed. Explain low-pass, high-pass and band-pass behaviour from H(ω). Some syllabi call this frequency-domain system analysis. Leave Laplace transfer function and pole-zero stability to Unit 4.

figure.aria: The RC low-pass magnitude is 1 at zero frequency and falls to 0.707 at ω=1000 rad/s.

chapters.example: An RC low-pass has R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF. Find H(ω) and the output for input 5 cos(1000t) V. Answer: RC=10³×10^{-6}=10^{-3} s; H(ω)=1/(1+j0.001ω). At ω=1000 rad/s H=1/(1+j1)=0.707∠−45°, so y(t)=3.54 cos(1000t−45°) V.
chapters.trap: Treating H(ω) as h(t), or ignoring phase when only magnitude is asked for sinusoidal output.
chapters.leave: Laplace transfer function and poles/zeros to Unit 4; BIBO proof to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A channel is distortionless when its magnitude is flat and its phase is linear; ideal brick-wall filters meet this but cannot be built exactly.
chapters.depth: State distortionless conditions: |H(ω)|=K constant and ∠H(ω)=−ωt_d linear over the signal band, so y(t)=Kx(t−t_d). Distinguish amplitude distortion from phase or delay distortion. Define ideal low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop filters with brick-wall magnitude and linear phase. Show ideal low-pass h(t) is a sinc extending from −∞ to ∞, so it is noncausal; exact ideal filters are not realizable. Explain practical filters by tolerance, transition band and delay. Mention the Paley–Wiener condition in words. Some syllabi call this distortion-free transmission and realizability of frequency response.

figure.title: Distortionless and ideal
figure.aria: A distortionless channel has flat magnitude and linear phase; an ideal brick-wall filter is a limiting case whose sinc impulse response is approximated in practice.

chapters.example: An ideal filter has gain K=2 and delay t_d=1 ms over |ω|≤2000 rad/s, with zero outside. Input x(t)=cos(1000t). Find output. Answer: ω=1000 is within band; H=2e^{-j0.001ω}; at ω=1000 phase=−1 rad; y(t)=2cos(1000t−1) V.
chapters.trap: Checking only flat |H(ω)|; a nonlinear phase still distorts the waveform.
chapters.leave: Filter design approximations beyond tolerance; sampling anti-alias filters to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Correlation measures similarity versus lag, and its Fourier transform is the spectral density.
chapters.depth: Define autocorrelation R_x(τ)=∫x(t)x(t+τ)dt for energy signals and the time-average version for power signals; define cross-correlation R_xy(τ). State properties: R_x(0)=E, |R_x(τ)|≤R_x(0), R_x(−τ)=R_x(τ) for real x. State Wiener–Khinchin: R_x(τ) ↔ |X(ω)|² for energy signals and ↔ PSD for power signals. Use correlation to measure similarity and delay. Some syllabi call spectral density the energy or power spectrum. Leave random-process correlation to later courses.

figure.aria: The autocorrelation of e^{-2t}u(t) peaks at τ=0 with value 0.25 and decays symmetrically for positive and negative lag.

chapters.example: Find the autocorrelation R_x(τ) and its Fourier transform for x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t). Answer: R_x(τ)=∫x(t)x(t+τ)dt; for τ≥0, R=e^{-2τ}/4; by symmetry R=e^{-2|τ|}/4. Its Fourier transform is 1/(4+ω²), which equals |X(ω)|².
chapters.trap: Using R_x(τ)=∫x(t)x(t−τ)dt with a sign error; autocorrelation is even for real signals.
chapters.leave: Random-process spectral estimation; DFT correlation to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The Hilbert transform is a 90° phase-shift filter that creates the quadrature signal and the analytic signal.
chapters.depth: Define Hilbert transform x̂(t)=(1/π)PV∫x(τ)/(t−τ)dτ. State frequency response H_H(ω)=−j sgn(ω): magnitude 1, phase −90° for positive frequencies and +90° for negative frequencies. Cover properties: linearity, energy preservation, orthogonality of x and x̂, double transform H{H{x}}=−x, and transform pairs cos→sin, sin→−cos for positive ω₀. Define analytic signal x_a(t)=x(t)+jx̂(t) in one line. Some syllabi include this as an advanced topic. Leave the discrete Hilbert transform out.

figure.aria: The Hilbert transform of a cosine is a sine, which is a −90° phase shift in this plot.

chapters.example: Find the Hilbert transform of x(t)=cos(ω₀t). Answer: X(ω)=π[δ(ω−ω₀)+δ(ω+ω₀)]; multiply by −j sgn(ω). For ω₀>0 this gives x̂(t)=sin(ω₀t).
chapters.trap: Choosing the sign of the 90° shift; under e^{-jωt} convention H{cos(ω₀t)}=sin(ω₀t), not −sin(ω₀t).
chapters.leave: Discrete Hilbert transform and analytic-signal applications beyond one line.
